clips.text_en_c1: Forced to select a single asset to hold over a ten-year horizon, would you gravitate toward Bitcoin or physical gold? The /biz/ thread essentially frames the dilemma as a clash between traditional store-of-value orthodoxy and the contemporary doctrine of digital scarcity. Most respondents remain firmly split: gold advocates emphasise millennia of monetary precedent and resilience against systemic shocks, whereas Bitcoin maximalists counter that programmable, capped supply represents a categorically superior hedge. Holding both simultaneously, meanwhile, has proven financially ruinous for the present commentator, who finds himself underwater on either position.
clips.text_en_c2: The hypothetical of holding a single asset for the ensuing decade elicits, predictably, the full spectrum of post-hoc rationalisation. Bitcoin partisans invoke its digitally native scarcity and the reflexive tendency of capital to chase momentum only after the move has already occurred, a structural inefficiency that should, in theory, persist. Gold advocates counter with a millennia-old track record of monetary legitimacy and the glacial, almost contemptuous, pace at which it accrues value. The respondent, who admits to losing money on both, occupies the uncomfortable epistemic ground of someone who has mastered the rhetoric without capturing the returns. Such is the retail condition.

clips.text_en_b2: The poster makes a fairly blunt point: if AI were genuinely about to displace workers on a massive scale, governments worldwide would already be scrambling to roll out universal basic income. Yet not a single administration has lifted a finger, which suggests to him that AI will probably wipe out well under one percent of jobs. Reassuring for anyone studying engineering, less so for everyone else hanging on by a thread.
clips.text_en_c1: The original poster advances a provocative syllogism: if artificial intelligence genuinely possessed the transformative labour-displacing capabilities its evangelists claim, governments worldwide would already be convening emergency sessions to negotiate universal basic income. Yet no administration, anywhere, has moved with any discernible urgency, which the OP interprets as conclusive evidence that the technology will displace considerably less than one percent of existing occupations. Pursuing a career in engineering, by that reasoning, ought to remain comparatively insulated. The author, for his part, acknowledges his own dependence on AI tools to compensate for what he self-deprecatingly describes as baseline intellectual inadequacy.
clips.text_en_c2: The original poster advances an elegantly counterintuitive argument: if artificial intelligence genuinely threatened mass white-collar displacement, every competent government on the planet would be in advanced negotiations over a universal basic income framework. Yet not one has moved with any urgency, which is taken as dispositive evidence that the labour-market apocalypse is largely theatrical. The implication is that the entire AI-job-loss discourse captures, at most, a sliver of one percent of the occupational landscape. The poster, a self-described engineering aspirant whose own productivity is somewhat embarrassingly dependent on the very technology in question, acknowledges the irony without quite resolving it.

clips.text_en_c1: The /v/ thread poses a deliberately provocative question: should game developers revert to hirsute, ruggedly masculine archetypes reminiscent of Wolverine, or persist with the smoother, more androgynous protagonists epitomised by Link? Opinions remain sharply polarised, with one faction championing a return to what they term authentic masculine aesthetics, and the other dismissing such preferences as reactionary. The respondent confesses an enduring affinity for the manlier archetype, noting that even during his fifteenth consecutive ranked climb, he instinctively gravitates toward imposing virtual companions. Studying for professional examinations yields a parallel phenomenon: he consistently conjures a suitably hardened imaginary mentor for moral support.
clips.text_en_c2: The proposition is straightforward enough: should game designers resurrect the lupine, weather-beaten masculinity epitomised by Wolverine, or persist with the lithe, almost androgynous figures exemplified by Link? /v/ remains, as ever, irreducibly divided. One camp craves the return of the hirsute protagonist, a compensatory fantasy whose appeal lies partly in the unavailability of such archetypes in contemporary life. The other treats Link as something approaching Platonic, an ur-form against which subsequent design choices are inevitably measured. The author, who has lately spent more time grinding ranked matches than he cares to admit, professes a clear preference and then, characteristically, extends the metaphor into domains where it rather conspicuously does not belong.
